content.p: Lucy Letby is a former neonatal nurse serving whole-life prison sentences for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more on the neonatal unit of the Countess of Chester Hospital in northern England between June 2015 and June 2016. She was convicted at Manchester Crown Court in August 2023, and a second jury convicted her of one further attempted murder in July 2024. The Guardian reported on her sentencing that she will never be released from prison.

The convictions remain in force, and two attempts to overturn them in the Court of Appeal have failed. Since 2024 the case has also become one of the most argued-over in modern British law: a group of medical experts says the evidence did not show murder, her lawyers have asked the Criminal Cases Review Commission to send the case back to the Court of Appeal, and a public inquiry reported in September 2026 on how the hospital responded. Letby has always denied harming any child in her care.

Letby was born in Hereford on 4 January 1990, the daughter of a furniture retail manager and an accounts clerk, according to a Yahoo profile. She studied nursing at the University of Chester, qualified in 2011 and started at the Countess of Chester Hospital the following year. She was a neonatal nurse, trained to care for premature and seriously ill babies, including those in intensive care. In 2016 the hospital took her off the neonatal unit.

A rise in infant deaths at the hospital brought scrutiny of her behaviour. Police arrested her in July 2018 on suspicion of murdering eight babies and attempting to murder six others, and released her on bail. She was arrested and released again in 2019. After a third arrest in November 2020 she was charged with the murder of eight babies between 2015 and 2016 and with ten counts of attempted murder.
content.h2: What the prosecution told the jury
content.p: The BBC reporter Stephanie Hegarty, who made a podcast on the case, told NPR that no one ever saw Letby commit a crime and that, rather than forensic evidence, the prosecution relied on medical evidence, such as the babies' medical and nursing notes. Prosecutors argued that Letby harmed babies in several ways. According to reports of the trial, these included injecting air, overfeeding with milk and poisoning with insulin. In the Guardian's summary of the evidence, seven babies were killed with air injected into them, two others were targeted through insulin added to their feeds, and a boy was attacked with a feeding tube forced down his throat.

The prosecution's leading expert witness was a retired consultant paediatrician, Dr Dewi Evans. The trial was told that Letby often attacked babies moments after their parents or other nurses had left their sides. Prosecutors also said that notes found at her home included the words "I AM EVIL I DID THIS" and another reading "I killed them on purpose because I'm not good enough to care for them". McDonald, her barrister, has since said he holds psychologists' reports on what was presented to the jury as a confession, and that it was not a confession at all.

Nicholas Johnson KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that Letby enjoyed "playing God" and was "excited" by the drama as doctors rushed to save the babies. The Guardian reported that the motive remained unclear. The judge declined to speculate on her reasons, saying they were "known only to you".

The first trial ran for about ten months, from October 2022 to August 2023. The jury found Letby guilty of seven counts of murder and seven of attempted murder, the attempts involving six babies, with two attempts on one child. The jury could not reach a verdict in the case of a baby referred to in court as Child K, and a second jury heard that charge at a retrial at Manchester Crown Court in 2024.

Sentence was passed on Monday 21 August 2023. Letby refused to leave her cell to hear it. Mr Justice Goss called her crimes a "cruel, calculated and cynical campaign of child murder involving the smallest and most vulnerable of children". He told her there was "a deep malevolence bordering on sadism in your actions" and that there were no mitigating factors. He gave her whole-life orders, reserved for crimes of exceptional gravity. The Guardian noted that Letby was the third woman alive to receive such a term, alongside Rose West and Joanna Dennehy. Parents of the victims spoke in court. One mother called Letby's absence "one final act of wickedness from a coward". A father said that the deaths of his two identical triplet sons had split his family and left him suicidal. One surviving girl, aged seven by the time of sentencing, was described as blind and as having quadriplegic cerebral palsy.

At the retrial, jurors were told that Child K was attacked in the early hours of 17 February 2016. Jurors were told that Letby dislodged the baby's breathing tube, and that a consultant, Dr Ravi Jayaram, walked in at about 3.45 a.m. and found her standing by the incubator, so that she was caught "virtually red-handed". Jayaram said he saw no sign that she was helping the baby. Letby told the court she had no recollection of the event and did not accept it had happened. The jury took three and a half hours to convict her. A 15th whole-life order followed, with the judge describing "another shocking act of calculated, callous cruelty". As she was led away she said, "I'm innocent."

Letby's first attempt to challenge her convictions failed in May 2024, when the Court of Appeal dismissed her challenge to the verdicts from her first trial. Her second came after the retrial. In October 2024 her barrister Benjamin Myers KC argued that media coverage before the retrial had been "saturated with unadulterated vitriol towards Ms Letby" and that the trial should have been stopped as an abuse of process. The CPS called the application "misguided". Three judges, Lord Justice William Davis, Lord Justice Jeremy Baker and Mrs Justice McGowan, refused permission, with Davis giving the ruling, saying the trial judge had been right to find that she could have a fair trial. He added that the application had raised a narrow legal issue and that nothing in the ruling could "contribute to any debate about the wider case against Lucy Letby".
content.h2: The challenge to the medical evidence
content.p: Questions about the evidence have multiplied since the trial ended. By September 2024 Letby had a new defence team headed by Mark McDonald, who told the BBC there was a strong case that she is innocent and that new medical evidence, hospital statistics and expert analysis revealed holes in the case against her. These are his claims.

In February 2025 an international panel of 14 clinicians, led by the neonatologist Dr Shoo Lee, held a news conference. The panel said it had found no medical evidence that Letby had injected air into babies or committed murder. "In all cases death or injury were due to natural causes or just bad medical care," Lee said. Lee also said that a 1989 research paper he wrote on air embolism in newborns, which Evans cited, was misrepresented at the trial. According to The BMJ, as cited by Yahoo, Lee was not asked to give evidence at the time and learned of the use of his research afterwards. Another panel member, Professor Neena Modi, wrote in The Guardian that the jury was told the babies were mostly healthy, whereas in her view they were overtly unwell or at high risk of complications.

The defence has pressed other points. In March 2025 the Telegraph reported that Letby's lawyers would give the Criminal Cases Review Commission 11 pieces of evidence. These included expert reports, comments by Dr Evans that the lawyers said arguably undermined his independence as an expert witness, and alleged failures by the prosecution to disclose evidence to the defence. The lawyers wrote that "there is now substantial evidence that undermines all the convictions".

Others have pushed back. The lawyer Peter Skelton, who acted for a number of the families, told the inquiry that what had been presented "with great fanfare as new and incontrovertible evidence turns out to be old and full of analytical holes". Andrew Kennedy KC, for the hospital, told the inquiry that the convictions stand and have been tested in two unsuccessful appeals.

Only the Criminal Cases Review Commission can send the case back to the Court of Appeal after the two refusals. It received an application for Letby on the evening of Monday 3 February 2025. The body said it was not for it to decide guilt or innocence, a matter for the courts, and that it could refer a case only if new evidence or argument raised "a real possibility" that a conviction would not be upheld. It warned that a significant volume of complicated evidence had been presented at her trials and that it could not say how long a review would take.

Letby's lawyers wrote in March 2025 that the commission was likely not to take long to consider the application. When CNN reported on 15 September 2026, Lady Justice Thirlwall said the commission was still working on it. The Guardian reported in April 2026 that the commission had been looking at evidence said to raise doubt about her guilt ever since February 2025.

The government ordered a public inquiry into how the hospital had responded. It opened at Liverpool Town Hall on 10 September 2024. Lady Justice Thirlwall said at the start that it was not for her to review the conviction: "the Court of Appeal has done that – the convictions stand". The inquiry could not make findings of civil or criminal liability.

In March 2025 Letby's lawyers asked Lady Justice Thirlwall to pause the inquiry until the Criminal Cases Review Commission had decided, and Sir David Davis and lawyers for former hospital managers made similar requests. Kate Blackwell, for the managers, said there now appeared to be a real likelihood of alternative explanations such as poor clinical care and natural causes. The hospital's lawyer said a pause would delay recommendations that were needed. The Care Quality Commission apologised to families for not showing enough "professional curiosity" about why baby deaths had risen.

Lady Justice Thirlwall published her report on Tuesday 15 September 2026, more than a year after hearings ended in March 2025. She described "dysfunctional management and governance, a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians, and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding", and "complete failure at all levels to invoke safeguarding procedures at any point". She concluded that "some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier". Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said she was "profoundly sorry" and announced plans for "cot cams" in neonatal units, and the hospital's chief executive, Jane Tomkinson, apologised. The report had no direct bearing on the convictions. CNN noted that Letby's supporters might use its findings of hospital failure to argue that systemic failures were partly to blame.

Cheshire Police opened an inquiry in October 2023 into possible corporate manslaughter at the hospital, called Operation Duet. In March 2025 it was widened to include gross negligence manslaughter by individuals. The Guardian reported in April 2026 that three former senior leaders of the hospital had been arrested in June 2025 on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter, and that one of them was arrested on 22 April 2026 on suspicion of perverting the course of justice and bailed. The force said both strands of the investigation were continuing, without set timescales. The Guardian noted that contempt of court restrictions apply to material that could prejudice a jury that may consider any charges.

The police also examined whether Letby harmed other babies. In January 2026 prosecutors announced that she would not face further charges. The file the CPS reviewed covered 11 new offences: two of murder and two of attempted murder relating to two babies who died, and seven of attempted murder relating to seven who survived. The CPS decided that the evidence did not meet the test for charging.

At 36, Letby is serving her sentences in prison. A Netflix documentary, The Investigation of Lucy Letby, was streaming by September 2026. As of the latest reports in September 2026, her lawyers say the babies died naturally, lawyers for some of the families dispute that, and the one body that can reopen her case is still weighing the application.
